episode.title: Cariboo Signals - Science, Wonder & the Natural World
episode.description:
Riley and Casey explore technology and society in rural communities. Today's focus: Science, Wonder & the Natural World.

THIS WEEK WE'RE ASKING: How much should neighbours know about each other?

NEWS ROUNDUP: We break down 100 Mile Ford running community coat drive for third year in a row and Former attorney general calls for B.C. Conservatives to continue to back AI reforms, plus 9 more stories, and explore what these developments mean for communities like ours.

RURAL CONNECTIONS: When a long-running observational record goes quiet, who should write the note explaining the silence, and how can a gap be distinguished from a genuinely quiet sky or system? Topics include: Inferred versus observed exoplanet evidence and the TOI-2535 b companion, Gap notation and the difference between silence, outage, and absence of data (Voyager 1 carrier versus science data), Synchrony in lake records and whether it signals climate forcing or systemic risk, Privacy, rules, and governance of a neighbour's creek camera recording animals and people, Who should write the explanation for a gap in a long observational record.

Hosts: Riley (Tech optimist with an engineering background) and Casey (Community-first skeptic of tech promises).

COMMUNITY SPOTLIGHT: Cariboo Chilcotin Conservation Society

discussion.central_question: When a long-running observational record goes quiet, who should write the note explaining the silence, and how can a gap be distinguished from a genuinely quiet sky or system?
discussion.riley_position: Silences in long records are open parts of the record rather than failures; the record should explicitly mark what it could not see, with the expected pattern, known gaps, and reasons stated beside it, and a camera on a creek can serve as a monitoring station if its purpose and data rules are set in advance.
riley_key_evidence: TESS watched TOI-2535 b from April 2019 to March 2026, with transits arriving up to six hours early or late before stopping, and an inferred companion planet detected via NEID spectrograph timing analysis.
Kepler-413b stopped transiting for 800 days under the influence of its two stars, providing precedent for disappearing transits.

Voyager 1 has sent no science data since November 14th, but its carrier signal was used on November 18th to confirm it was about one light-day (roughly 16 billion miles) from Earth, and a similar 2023 interruption was resolved with science data returning in June 2024.
discussion.casey_position: Records are only as trustworthy as the people writing their gap notes, so a log kept by the person who lost the data is a self-report; the rules for any monitoring, especially cameras recording neighbours, must be written down before disputes arise, and synchrony in lake data may reflect shared climate forcing rather than new systemic fragility.
casey_key_evidence: The TOI-2535 b companion is inferred from timing, not yet seen, and the press coverage headlined it as an "invisible planet" while the paper called it inferred.
Voyager's commands take a day each way, and project manager Suzanne Dodd expects more anomalies as the probes age, even while expressing confidence in a fix.

A PNAS study of about 2,000 lakes found temperature, algal blooms and oxygen increasingly moving together across continents, which Casey notes could stem from regional weather and warming air rather than new fragility.
discussion.resolution: They agreed that the record should explicitly state what it could not see and that a gap note should not be written solely by the person who lost the data, but they disagreed on who should write it, with Riley proposing a body holding the log or a later reader checking the raw data, and Casey insisting the rules be written before anyone has reason to dispute them. The question was left open.

research.block:
PRE-RESEARCHED INSIGHTS FOR THE DEEP DIVE

RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the Voyager 1 data outage a minor glitch or a serious threat to the mission, and what is the current status?
Findings: NASA's Voyager team says the spacecraft stopped sending science and engineering data on November 14. Mission engineers first noticed this when a Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, locked onto the probe and received its carrier signal. The carrier is strong, but the spacecraft currently lacks frame sync, so no usable science or engineering data is coming through. Project manager Suzanne Dodd called it "an anomaly that is not something unseen before." Space.com reports that the team remains in contact with the probe while it investigates and is confident it can solve the problem. Live Science notes a similar computer-related problem came up as recently as 2024. The one-light-day milestone was reached on November 18, when the probe was roughly 16 billion miles away and its signal took 24 hours to reach Earth.
Suggested angle: Riley can argue this is the best evidence for engineering resilience: a 1977 probe, now beyond the reach of any repair crew, is still transmitting a carrier signal, and its team has fixed similar faults before. Casey can counter that "still beaming a signal" is not the same as "doing science," and that the distance itself means every fix takes days of round-trip commanding, so the mission's margin is shrinking. The 2024 precedent cuts both ways. Use it to ask whether one more unprecedented anomaly is a fair test of how much longer a 50-year-old machine can last.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Does the UBC/Sheffield claim that QCD vacuum physics could explain dark energy stand on solid ground, and how much is still open?
Findings: The work is led by Dong Ha Lee, a PhD student at the University of Sheffield, with UBC co-authors. The paper was published in The Astrophysical Journal (IOPscience, DOI 10.3847/1538-4357/aeb9cc) and posted to arXiv as "Evolving Dark Energy Is Vacuum Energy After All." The authors describe dark energy as arising from a topological contribution to the QCD vacuum energy, linked to the global structure of the gauge field. Press materials say the model reproduces the observed dark-energy scale from known constants of QCD and gravity, without new particles or additional fitting parameters. The paper frames itself as a model of dynamical, evolving dark energy. The UBC press framing is cautious: the team says the idea is "very intriguing," and the phys.org headline frames it as "rival accounts," meaning this is one proposal among several. I did not find independent replication or a published critique in my searches, so the claim has been peer-reviewed but not yet independently confirmed.
Suggested angle: Riley can use this as an example of physics showing that a mystery may not need exotic new particles, since a known force might be doing the work. Casey can press on the word "could." A model that matches the observed scale without tuning is a striking claim, but matching one number is different from making testable predictions that rival models cannot. The useful question for the debate is what observation would prove this model wrong, and whether it predicts a specific evolution of dark energy that future surveys can check.

RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the "lakes syncing up globally" finding an established result, and what is the strongest objection to the alarm in the coverage?
Findings: The study is by Ke Zhang and colleagues, published in PNAS (DOI 10.1073/pnas.2611874123; online November 16, 2026; issue dated November 24). It analyzes long-term records from about 2,000 lakes and finds that ecological conditions such as temperature, algal blooms, and oxygen levels are increasingly moving together across continents. The authors call this "an emergent property of the Anthropocene" and argue it erodes the spatial variety that historically buffered regional environmental shocks. Coverage such as 404 Media's frames this as a warning, and Above the Norm News says researchers warn of possible collapses on several continents at once. The paper itself is more measured in its language. It describes a trend and an interpretation, not a demonstrated collapse risk. Coverage also repeats that lakes are mainly managed locally or regionally.
Suggested angle: Casey can argue that synchrony is not the same as fragility. Lakes may be moving together mainly because they share the same large-scale drivers, such as regional weather patterns and warming air temperatures, which would make the trend a signal of climate forcing rather than a new system-level vulnerability. Riley can respond that even if the cause is shared climate forcing, a world where lakes respond in unison is one where global satellite monitoring can spot problems early and where management must shift from local to planetary scale. The debate turns on whether the synchrony is a warning about fragility or a sign that we finally have the data to see the whole system.

roundup.opening_frame: A day that opens with local kindness and a hard question about AI accountability, then turns to a news day of deep-time fossils, shifting climates and stars colliding.

stories.point: 100 Mile Ford is on track to collect over 100 jackets in the KOT Auto Group's eighth annual Coat Drive, its third year taking part, with donations going to the Cariboo Christian Life Fellowship church in the 108 Mile Ranch area at the end of November.

B.C.'s former attorney general Niki Sharma is urging the incoming Conservative government to keep backing Criminal Code changes for AI accountability and to see the province's lawsuit against OpenAI through, after Mother Jones published more details of the Tumbler Ridge shooter's ChatGPT logs.

A Nature study dates the Taung Child fossil to about 2.96 to 3.03 million years ago and suggests the human family tree in southern Africa was more branched than assumed, with some fossils once grouped as one species possibly representing different branches.
Researchers in China's Yunnan Province have described Dianjunus rex, a giant fungus up to 20 inches tall and nearly 5 pounds, which forms an entirely new family with no known close relatives.
A Nature study modelling future drought finds most of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate changes, and more than a quarter could lose at least 80 percent of it by 2100.

Two Nature studies report that Homo erectus lived in southern China from about 324,000 to 184,000 years ago, roughly 200,000 years later than the known mainland Asian record, in a rainforest habitat, and a ninth tooth matches none of the known human groups.

Paleontologists have formally named Vampyrocamelus welshi, a long-legged, giraffe-like camel from about 13 million years ago, from museum fossils found mainly in Texas and Oklahoma, though what its large backward-curving teeth were for remains uncertain.
A study that recorded brainwaves and eye movements of humans and macaques watching Minions clips and nature documentaries shows how primate brains make meaning out of visual scenes.

A global analysis finds glaciers ending in lakes lost ice faster from 2000 to 2020 than land- or marine-ending glaciers, with 3,567 more ice-contact lakes by 2020, and a Cambridge researcher calls for tiered safety oversight of hazardous glacial lakes.

Earlier this week: a University of Bath study estimates human metabolism produces about 2.05 billion metric tons of CO2 a year, up 74% from 1985 to 2015 mostly through population growth, and is a different thing from fossil-fuel emissions.

Sediment cores show the Amazon had virtually no wildfires through the last glacial period until humans arrived, so its plants never evolved fire defences, and this season's peak El Niño coinciding with the dry season could push the forest to a breaking point.

Earlier this week: Nautilus looked back at the Victorian-era X Club of British scientists who helped shift universities toward independent research, a change Cambridge marked with sabbaticals in 1926.
A Nature study shows Earth's magnetic field guides Australia's bogong moths on their migration of up to 1,000 kilometres when starlight fails.

Webb observed AT 2025abao in the Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiralled into a red giant and merged over about seven years, and the findings suggest energy transport during the shared-envelope phase is more complex than standard models say.

Four Australian researchers wrote their own imaging algorithm, ran it on the same data, and recovered a ring nearly identical to the 2019 Event Horizon Telescope image of the M87 black hole, the first truly independent check of that result.

A University of Sydney-led study finds masers assigned to the Milky Way's Norma arm line up with a shock front from the galaxy's central bar, so part of the supposed arm may be a star-forming region along the bar.
An Oregon State study in npj Microgravity used simulated moon soil mixed with worm-made vermicompost to work out a baseline recipe for growing potatoes for future lunar colonists.

roundup.handoff: A long run of stories about things seen, re-checked and re-measured, leaving the listener asking what happens when the thing doing the watching goes quiet.

deep_dive.central_question: When a long-running watcher of the sky or of the land goes quiet, is the silence itself a finding, as with the planet that vanished from TESS's view, or only a gap that the record has to admit it cannot read, as with Voyager 1?
deep_dive.riley_holds: Silence in a well-kept record can be informative, because the planet's disappearance from seven years of TESS data pointed to an unseen companion, so the sensible move is to keep watching and learn to read gaps.
deep_dive.casey_holds: A gap is not evidence of anything until someone shows what caused it, and an unseen companion or a dead probe computer is an explanation offered after the fact, so records must mark what they could not see rather than let silence be read as a result.

beats.claim: A planet disappearing from view became the discovery, because the record was long and unbroken enough to show what normal looked like.
beats.evidence: TESS watched TOI-2535 b from April 2019 to March 2026. Before the transits stopped they arrived up to six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, which astronomers read as a changing orbit tilt. They attribute it to a nearby unseen planet's pull, and the planet is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years (popsci.com, skyatnightmagazine.com, universetoday.com). Samuel Yee says the universe is not regular clockwork (Futurism).
beats.pushback: Casey: the companion is still unseen, inferred from timing and a NEID spectrograph analysis, and how the hot Jupiter got so close to its star remains uncertain, so the vanishing is a clue and not a proven cause. Riley can answer that the companion could transit sooner, which would test it (popsci.com).
beats.leads_to_next: If a vanishing signal can be a clue, the question is whether every silence can be read that way, and Voyager 1's silence is the test case.

beats.claim: Not every silence is a finding: when Voyager 1 stopped returning data, the honest reading is a fault under investigation, and the record has to say so.
beats.evidence: Voyager 1 has sent no science or engineering data since Nov. 14, though its carrier signal remains detectable and let engineers verify it reached one light-day (about 16 billion miles) on Nov. 18. A 2023 computer failure was fixed in June 2024, and project manager Suzanne Dodd expects more anomalies as the probes age (nasa.gov, livescience.com).
beats.pushback: Riley: silence has degrees, since the carrier signal still confirms the craft is transmitting and its distance, and the earlier gap was repaired, so a gap can be labelled by what is still known rather than treated as blank. Casey accepts the carrier signal confirms distance but not the missing science readings.
beats.leads_to_next: If gaps come in kinds, the next question is how a record shows which kind it holds, and the lakes study shows how much a long record can reveal when it is kept.

beats.claim: Some truths exist only as patterns across a long record, and they are invisible to any single snapshot or any single lake.
beats.evidence: A PNAS study of satellite imagery of roughly 2,000 lakes since 2000 finds lakes increasingly synchronised in warming, algal blooms and oxygen levels, which authors describe as a genuine global-scale phenomenon and a possible fundamental reorganisation of lake systems. Lake-to-lake diversity normally buffers damage (404 Media).
beats.pushback: Casey: the authors themselves call the reorganisation a possibility, and a headline calling it a warning runs ahead of what satellites measured on lake surfaces. Riley accepts the hedge but says it only shows the record must stay open so the claim can be checked or retired.
beats.leads_to_next: If patterns only show over years, whoever keeps the log carries the burden of marking when it was not watching, which brings the idea home to a Cariboo sky.

beats.claim: A rural dark-sky or aurora log is only as readable as its marked gaps: a clear night with no aurora, a cloudy night and a night nobody looked are three different entries.
beats.evidence: Draws on the TESS case, where early and late transits meant something only against an expected schedule, and on Voyager, where a carrier signal could be read as distance but not as science. Callback to Oct. 11, when the hosts left open who should hold a Chilcotin sky-count protocol.
beats.leads_to_next: If the log must mark its gaps, the last beat asks who should be trusted to write that mark and how readers can tell a quiet sky from an unwatched one.

beats.claim: Reading silence responsibly needs three things written beside any long record: the expected pattern, the known gaps, and the reason for each gap.
beats.evidence: TOI-2535 b's anomalies were readable because the expected transit times were known. Voyager's team separated the carrier signal from the missing science data. The lake study's claim rests on a stated baseline of 2,000 lakes since 2000 (popsci.com, nasa.gov, 404 Media).
beats.pushback: Casey: a gap note written by the same people who lost the data is a self-report, and a 30-year wait for a transit means no one living may check it. Riley concedes this and says the companion could show up sooner.
beats.leads_to_next: That leaves the landing: who writes the gap note, and who can challenge it.

set_aside: Dark energy rival models (UBC/Sheffield QCD and Ottawa CCC+TL): a theory comparison with no watcher or record to read
deep_dive.cariboo_beat: Beat 4 brings it to the dark rural skies of the Cariboo, where aurora and star counts kept by local sky-watchers are only readable if clouded-out and unwatched nights are marked, picking up Oct. 11's open Chilcotin protocol question in one line.
deep_dive.landing: Held open: when a long record of the sky or land goes quiet, who should write the note that says why, the person who kept it, a body that holds it, or a later reader checking it, and how can anyone tell a quiet sky from a night nobody was watching.
